x.Darby: A Song of degrees. Of Solomon. Unless Jehovah build the house, in vain do its builders labour in it; unless Jehovah keep the city, the keeper watcheth in vain:
x.KJV: A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the Lord keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
x.YLT: A Song of the Ascents, by Solomon. If Jehovah doth not build the house, In vain have its builders laboured at it, If Jehovah doth not watch a city, In vain hath a watchman waked.

nt: This phrase introduces the consequence of the condition proposed in the previous phrase. Use a natural form in your language for introducing the consequence of this possible condition. Alternate translation: [then it does not help for its builders to labor on it]

This phrase introduces the consequence of the condition proposed in the previous phrase. Use a natural form in your language for introducing the consequence of this possible condition. Alternate translation: [then it does no good for the watchman to stand guard over it]

x.ASV: It is vain for you to rise up early, To take rest late, To eat the bread of toil; For so he giveth unto his beloved sleep.
x.Darby: It is vain for you to rise up early, to lie down late, to eat the bread of sorrows: so to his beloved one he giveth sleep.
x.KJV: It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep.
x.YLT: Vain for you who are rising early, Who delay sitting, eating the bread of griefs, So He giveth to His beloved one sleep.

nt: Solomon is referring to all of a person’s working time by naming two extremes, **the ones rising early to get up** and **the ones being late to sit down**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the ones working from early morning until late at night]

Solomon is speaking of working hard to raise the food that people eat as if it were **bread of toils**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those toiling to earn your food]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **toils**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [bread gained by toiling]

Solomon is using the possessive form to describe **bread** that is characterized by **toils**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [bread earned through hard work]
The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh, who is named in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [certainly Yahweh gives to his beloved one sleep]

x.ASV: Lo, children are a heritage of Jehovah; And the fruit of the womb is his reward.
x.Darby: Lo, children are an inheritance from Jehovah, [and] the fruit of the womb a reward.
x.KJV: Lo, children are an heritage of the Lord: and the fruit of the womb is his reward.
x.YLT: Lo, an inheritance of Jehovah are sons, A reward is the fruit of the womb.

nt: Solomon is using the word **Behold** to focus the readers’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]
נַחֲלַ֣ת יְהוָ֣ה בָּנִ֑ים שָׂ֝כָ֗ר פְּרִ֣י הַ⁠בָּֽטֶן

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [what Yahweh gives as an inheritance is sons, indeed, the fruit of the womb is his reward]
If your language does not use abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what Yahweh gives as a gift]
If your language does not use abstract noun for the idea of **reward**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what he gives to reward you]

Solomon is using **fruit of the womb** as a common expression of his culture to mean “children” or “offspring.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is having children]

x.ASV: As arrows in the hand of a mighty man, So are the children of youth.
x.Darby: As arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the children of youth.
x.KJV: As arrows are in the hand of a mighty man; so are children of the youth.
x.YLT: As arrows in the hand of a mighty one, So are the sons of the young men.

nt: The point of this comparison is that just as **arrows** in the hand of a warrior are powerful and useful for defense, so **the sons** a man has in his youth can help defend a man from his enemies when he grows old. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [The sons of a man’s youth are a powerful defense and as useful as arrows in the hand of a warrior]

Solomon is using this possessive form to describe **sons** who were born during a man’s **youth**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [are sons born during one’s youth]

x.ASV: Happy is the man that hath his quiver full of them: They shall not be put to shame, When they speak with their enemies in the gate.
x.Darby: Happy is the man that hath filled his quiver with them. They shall not be ashamed when they speak with enemies in the gate.
x.KJV: Happy is the man that hath his quiver full of them: they shall not be ashamed, but they shall speak with the enemies in the gate.
x.YLT: O the happiness of the man Who hath filled his quiver with them, They are not ashamed, For they speak with enemies in the gate!

nt: Solomon is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy about the man who has many sons. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How happy is] or [Truly blessed is]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means any man in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [any man]

Solomon is continuing the arrow imagery from the previous verse, speaking of having many sons as if the father had **filled his quiver** with arrows. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [has been given many children]

A **quiver** is a container that a warrior carries on his back or at his side for holding arrows. If your readers would not be familiar with what a quiver is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [his arrow bag]

The pronoun **They** likely refers to men who have many sons. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The man who have many sons will not have shame when he speaks]

By **have shame**, Solomon means that they will not feel the shame of being defeated by the adversary. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [They will not feel the shame of defeat]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **shame**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [They will not be ashamed by being defeated]

Solomon assumes that his readers will know that **the gate** of a city was where important legal and public matters were discussed and settled. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the place where public disputes are settled]
